questions.question: What is polymorphism in Java and what are its two types?
questions.title: Polymorphism in Java — Compile-Time and Runtime
questions.direct_answer: Polymorphism means 'many forms'. In Java, it means one method name can behave differently depending on what object you call it on. Java has two types: **compile-time polymorphism** (method overloading — resolved at compile time based on parameter types) and **runtime polymorphism** (method overriding — resolved at runtime based on the actual object type).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of both types of polymorphism and what distinguishes them
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing overloading with overriding, or not knowing which one is compile-time vs runtime
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that runtime polymorphism is the more powerful and commonly used form — it's the foundation of OOP design patterns

sections.title: One Method Call, Many Behaviors — Decided at Two Different Times
sections.content:
**Polymorphism** means the same method call can do different things depending on which object actually runs it. The word comes from Greek and literally means 'many forms' — one name, many behaviors.

Why does Java need this? Without it, every time you wanted different behavior you would write a long chain of `if-else` or `switch` checks asking 'what type is this object?'. Polymorphism **removes those checks** — you call one method and the right version runs automatically.

Java gives you this in two ways. **Compile-time polymorphism** is **method overloading**: several methods share a name but take different parameters, and the *compiler* decides which one to call by looking at the arguments you pass. Because the decision is locked in before the program runs, it is also called **static binding**.

**Runtime polymorphism** is **method overriding**: a child class rewrites a method it inherited, and the *JVM* decides which version to run by looking at the actual object in memory — not the variable's declared type. This runtime lookup is called **dynamic method dispatch** or **dynamic binding**.

In interviews the **distinction that matters is when the choice is made**: overloading is resolved at compile time, overriding at runtime. And of the two, overriding is the one that powers real OOP design — it is what lets you write code against a parent type today and have it work for subclasses you haven't even created yet.

> The trap: overloading is picked from the *reference* type, while overriding is picked from the *actual* object.

sections.title: Compile-Time vs Runtime Polymorphism at a Glance
sections.content:
The two paths look very different in terms of *when* the method version is chosen.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["Polymorphism"] --> CT["Compile-Time Polymorphism"]
    P --> RT["Runtime Polymorphism"]

    CT --> CT1["Mechanism: Method Overloading"]
    CT1 --> CT2["Same class, same name, different params"]
    CT2 --> CT3["Compiler picks version from argument types"]
    CT3 --> CT4["Static binding — decided BEFORE the program runs"]

    RT --> RT1["Mechanism: Method Overriding"]
    RT1 --> RT2["Child class redefines parent method (same signature)"]
    RT2 --> RT3["JVM picks version from actual object type at runtime"]
    RT3 --> RT4["Dynamic binding — decided WHILE the program runs"]
```

The fork at the top is the key interview answer: two types, two different mechanisms, two different timings.

sections.title: Compile-Time vs Runtime Polymorphism
sections.content:
| Aspect | Compile-Time (Overloading) | Runtime (Overriding) |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Method overloading | Method overriding |
| When resolved | At compile time | At runtime |
| Binding type | Static binding | Dynamic binding |
| Requires inheritance | No — same class | Yes — parent-child |
| Parameters | Must differ | Must be identical |
| Return type | Can differ | Same or covariant |
| Purpose | API convenience | Extensible behavior |

sections.title: Both Types of Polymorphism — Animal.speak() and a Calculator
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mixing up overloading and overriding** — overloading is same class with different parameters; overriding is parent-and-child with the same signature. Swapping the two is the single most common fresher slip.
- **Forgetting which one is compile-time** — overloading is resolved by the compiler (static binding); overriding is resolved by the JVM at runtime (dynamic binding). Saying overriding happens at compile time is an instant red flag.
- **Assuming all polymorphism needs inheritance** — overriding does, but overloading lives inside one class and needs no parent at all.
- **Thinking the reference type chooses the overridden method** — for overriding, the *actual object* decides which version runs, never the declared variable type.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Polymorphism = 'many forms'** — one method name, many different behaviors depending on context.
- **Two types** — compile-time (overloading, static binding) and runtime (overriding, dynamic binding).
- **Overloading** — multiple methods, same name, different parameter lists in one class; compiler resolves at compile time.
- **Overriding** — child class redefines parent's method with the same signature; JVM resolves at runtime based on actual object.
- **Runtime polymorphism is more powerful** — it enables writing code against parent types that works for all current and future child types.
- **Memory hook** — overloading = same class + different params; overriding = parent-child + same signature.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd start with the idea, not the dictionary: the same method call lands on different behavior depending on the object behind it. Java does this two ways, and the line interviewers care about is **when the choice gets made**.

**Overloading is the compile-time kind** — same name, different parameters, and the `compiler` picks the version from the arguments you pass before the program runs. **Overriding is the runtime kind** — a child rewrites a parent's method, and the `JVM` picks the version from the real object in memory while the program runs.

People mix these up constantly, so I keep one rule:
- **Overloading** — same class plus different parameters
- **Overriding** — parent-child plus the same signature

Of the two, **overriding is the one that actually matters in design** — it's the foundation under patterns like Strategy and Template Method, because you write code against the parent type and it keeps working for subclasses you add years later.

questions.question: How does runtime polymorphism work with a parent reference pointing to a child object?
questions.title: Runtime Polymorphism — Parent Reference to Child Object
questions.direct_answer: When a parent reference holds a child object (`Animal a = new Dog()`), the reference type (`Animal`) controls which methods are *visible* at compile time, but the actual object type (`Dog`) controls which implementation *runs* at runtime. The JVM performs virtual method dispatch — it looks up the real object's class and calls its version of the method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of how the JVM resolves method calls at runtime vs compile time
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the reference type determines which method runs — it only determines which methods are visible; the object type determines execution
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the practical benefit: you can write code against the Animal type and it works correctly for all subclasses without modification — the Open/Closed Principle

sections.title: Why the Variable Type and the Object Type Do Two Different Jobs
sections.content:
**Runtime polymorphism** means that when you call a method through a parent reference, Java runs the version that belongs to the actual object — not the version that belongs to the reference type. The classic line is `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();` and it prints `'Woof!'`, the `Dog` version, even though the variable is declared as `Animal`.

The reason is that two separate types are doing two separate jobs. The **reference type** (`Animal`) is what the compiler sees. It acts as a gatekeeper: it decides which methods you are *allowed* to call. If you try `a.wagTail()` and `Animal` has no `wagTail()`, the code won't compile — even though the real object is a `Dog` that has it.

The **object type** (`Dog`) is what the JVM sees at runtime. When the line actually executes, the JVM ignores the variable's declared type, looks at the real object sitting in memory, finds that object's version of `speak()`, and runs it. This runtime lookup is called **dynamic method dispatch** or **dynamic binding** — and it's why this is called *runtime* polymorphism: the choice happens while the program runs, not before.

This is what makes **flexible code** possible. You can write one method like `makeAnimalSpeak(Animal a)` that calls `a.speak()`, then pass it a `Dog`, a `Cat`, or a `Bird` you write next month — each speaks correctly with no `instanceof` checks and no edits to the method. That's the **Open/Closed Principle**: open for extension, closed for modification.

Under the hood the JVM uses a **virtual method table (vtable)** per class — a lookup table mapping each method to its implementation. When a subclass overrides a method, its vtable entry points to the subclass version, so the JVM just follows the real object's vtable to land on the right code.

> One nuance worth knowing: dynamic dispatch applies to methods only. Fields are resolved by the reference type, so `a.someField` reads `Animal`'s field, never `Dog`'s — fields are not polymorphic.

sections.title: Virtual Method Dispatch — What Happens When You Call a.speak()
sections.content:
Trace the full journey from the source line to the output:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Animal a = new Dog()"] --> B["Variable 'a' has reference type: Animal"]
    A --> C["Object in memory is type: Dog"]

    B --> D["Compile time: compiler checks Animal has speak() — allowed"]
    C --> E["Runtime: JVM looks at actual object in memory"]

    E --> F{"What is the real class?"}
    F -->|"Dog"| G["Call Dog.speak() → prints 'Woof!'"]
    F -->|"Cat"| H["Call Cat.speak() → prints 'Meow!'"]
    F -->|"Animal (no override)"| I["Call Animal.speak() → generic sound"]

    G --> J["Output: Woof!"]
    H --> J2["Output: Meow!"]
    I --> J3["Output: Some generic animal sound"]
```

The compile-time check (left branch) only asks: *is the method allowed?* The runtime dispatch (right branch) asks: *which version should run?* These are two completely separate questions answered at two completely different times.

sections.title: Parent Reference, Child Behavior — Animal.speak() Example
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Believing the reference type decides which method runs** — it only controls visibility; the actual object type always decides execution. This is the heart of the question and the most common wrong answer.
- **Trying to call child-only methods through a parent reference** — `Animal a = new Dog(); a.wagTail();` won't compile; you must cast to `Dog` first.
- **Assuming fields are polymorphic too** — only methods are dispatched dynamically; field access uses the reference type, so `a.name` reads `Animal`'s field even when the object is a `Dog`.
- **Confusing this with overloading** — overloading is chosen by the compiler from argument types; this dispatch is chosen by the JVM from the real object at runtime.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Reference type controls visibility** — only methods defined on the reference type are accessible at compile time; child-specific methods require a cast.
- **Object type controls execution** — the JVM always dispatches to the actual object's class version of the method at runtime.
- **Virtual method dispatch** — the JVM mechanism that walks the actual object's vtable at runtime to find the correct method implementation.
- **Dynamic binding** — method calls are resolved at runtime, not compile time; this is what makes runtime polymorphism 'poly'.
- **Open/Closed Principle** — code written against the parent type (`Animal`) works automatically for all present and future subclasses without modification.
- **Cannot call child-specific methods** — `a1.wagTail()` fails to compile if `Animal` has no `wagTail()`; you must cast to `Dog` first.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The key mental model is that `Animal a = new Dog()` puts **two types in play**, and they do completely different jobs.

The **reference type** — `Animal` — is what the compiler checks. It's a gatekeeper for what you're allowed to call: if `Animal` has `speak()`, you can call it; if you try a `Dog`-only method like `wagTail()`, it won't compile, even though the real object is a `Dog`.

The **object type** — `Dog` — is what the JVM cares about when the program actually runs. At that point it ignores the declared type, looks at the real object in memory, finds `Dog`'s `speak()`, and runs it, so you get `'Woof!'` and not the `Animal` version. That runtime lookup is **dynamic method dispatch**, and the JVM does it through a `vtable` per class.

Why it matters in real code: you can write one method that takes an `Animal`, call `speak()` inside it, and pass it any animal you ever create — no `instanceof`, no if-else chains, and you never touch that method again when you add a new subclass. That's the **Open/Closed Principle** in practice. The mistake I'd be careful to avoid is saying the reference type picks the method — it doesn't, it only controls visibility. And a detail that usually impresses: **dynamic dispatch applies to methods only** — fields are resolved by the reference type, so fields are not polymorphic.

questions.question: What is method overloading in Java and what are the rules for it?
questions.title: Method Overloading Rules in Java
questions.direct_answer: Method overloading is defining multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler picks which version to call based on the number, type, or order of arguments. **Return type alone cannot distinguish overloaded methods** — that causes a compile error.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowing the rules for overloading and the common gotcha about return type
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you can overload by changing only the return type — this causes a compile error
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that overloading is resolved at compile time (static dispatch) and that auto-widening can cause surprising method selection

sections.title: Same Name, Different Parameters — and Why the Compiler Decides
sections.content:
**Method overloading** means having several methods with the same name in one class, each taking a different list of parameters. When you call the method, the compiler looks at the arguments you pass and picks the matching version.

Why is this useful? It lets **one clear name** handle related jobs instead of inventing `printInt`, `printString`, and `printDouble`. Java's own `System.out.println()` is the famous example — it has versions for `int`, `double`, `String`, `boolean`, `char`, and more, and you never think about which one you're calling.

There are exactly three ways to make a valid overload, all about the parameter list:
- **Different number of parameters** — `add(int a, int b)` versus `add(int a, int b, int c)`
- **Different parameter types** — `print(int n)` versus `print(String s)`
- **Different order of parameter types** — `log(String msg, int level)` versus `log(int level, String msg)`

> The rule almost every fresher trips on: you **cannot** overload by changing only the return type. `int getValue()` and `String getValue()` with the same parameters is a compile error, because when you call a method without using its result, the compiler would have no way to tell which one you meant.

How it's resolved is the part that earns points: overloading is decided at **compile time** from the static types at the call site — this is **static binding**, the opposite of overriding, which the JVM resolves at runtime. One subtlety interviewers probe is **auto-widening**: if you call `compute(5)` and there's no `compute(int)` but there is `compute(long)`, Java silently widens the `int` to `long` and picks that, which can produce surprising selections when several numeric overloads exist. The most common real-world use of all this is **constructor overloading** — giving callers several ways to build an object depending on what they have.

sections.title: What Makes a Valid Overload? — Side by Side
sections.content:
Three ways to make valid overloads, one way that always fails: ```mermaid flowchart TD M["Method name: add()"] --> V1["Valid: different number of params"] M --> V2["Valid: different param types"] M --> V3["Valid: different param order"] M --> INV["INVALID: different return type only"] V1 --> V1E["add(int a, int b)
add(int a, int b, int c)"] V2 --> V2E["add(int a, int b)
add(double a, double b)"] V3 --> V3E["log(String msg, int level)
log(int level, String msg)"] INV --> INVE["int get() { }
String get() { } ← compile error"] V1E --> R["Compiler picks correct version at compile time"] V2E --> R V3E --> R INVE --> ERR["Compiler cannot distinguish — error"] ```

sections.title: Valid vs Invalid Overloading — Quick Reference
sections.content:
| Scenario | Valid overload? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Different number of parameters | Yes | Compiler can count arguments |
| Different parameter types | Yes | Compiler checks argument types |
| Different parameter order | Yes | Compiler checks type sequence |
| Different return type only | **No — compile error** | Compiler can't distinguish on return type alone |
| Adding `throws` clause | No | Exception clause is not part of signature |
| Different access modifier only | No | Access modifier is not part of signature |

sections.title: Overloading in Action — Valid and Invalid Examples
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Overloading by return type alone** — same name and parameters but a different return type is always a compile error; the compiler can't choose when the result is ignored.
- **Thinking a different access modifier or `throws` clause makes an overload** — neither is part of the signature, so changing only those is a duplicate-method error.
- **Ignoring auto-widening** — calling `add(5)` when only `add(long)` exists silently promotes the `int`; with mixed numeric overloads you can hit a version you didn't expect.
- **Confusing overloading with overriding** — overloading is one class, different parameters, chosen by the compiler; overriding is parent-child, same signature, chosen by the JVM at runtime.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Method signature** = method name + parameter types in order. Return type is **not** part of the signature.
- **Three valid ways to overload** — different number of params, different param types, different param order.
- **Return type rule** — you cannot overload by changing only the return type. This is a compile error.
- **Static dispatch** — overloaded method selection happens at compile time based on the argument types at the call site.
- **Auto-widening** — if no exact parameter match exists, Java widens primitive types (`int → long → double`) to find the best match.
- **Constructor overloading** — the most common use case; provide multiple ways to initialize an object with different parameter combinations.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Overloading is just reusing one method name in a class for several methods that take different parameters, and letting the **compiler pick the right one** from the arguments you pass — `System.out.println` is the everyday example, with versions for `int`, `String`, `double`, and more.

There are three valid ways to vary it:
- a **different number** of parameters
- **different parameter types**
- a **different order** of types

The trap freshers fall into is thinking you can **overload on return type** — two methods with the same name and parameters but different return types won't compile, because if you call the method and ignore the result, the compiler has no way to know which one you meant.

The detail that sets an answer apart is naming *when* this happens: **overloading is resolved at compile time** (static binding), unlike overriding which the JVM resolves at runtime. I'd also flag **auto-widening** — call `add(5)` with only an `add(long)` around and Java quietly widens the `int` to `long`, which can pick a version you didn't expect when you've got several numeric overloads.

questions.question: What are the rules for method overriding in Java?
questions.title: Method Overriding Rules in Java
questions.direct_answer: For valid method overriding: the method must have the **same name and parameter list** as the parent method, the return type must be the same or a **covariant subtype**, the access modifier must be the same or **more permissive**, and checked exceptions must be the same or **narrower**. Private, static, and final methods cannot be overridden. Always use `@Override` to let the compiler verify.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of all the overriding rules, particularly covariant return types, access modifier widening, and exception rules
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about covariant return types, or thinking you can narrow the access modifier (e.g., parent public to child private)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @Override's role in catching typos and the covariant return type feature added in Java 5

sections.title: The Five Rules That Keep an Override From Silently Breaking
sections.content:
**Method overriding** means a child class replaces a method it inherited from its parent with its own version that has the same signature. It is the mechanism behind runtime polymorphism — the reason `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();` runs `Dog`'s code.

Java enforces strict rules so that a child object can always stand in for a parent object safely — that's the **Liskov Substitution Principle**. There are five to know.

**Rule 1 — the signature must match exactly.** Same method name, same parameter list. Get a parameter type wrong and you haven't overridden anything; you've accidentally created a *new overloaded* method, and the parent's version still runs through a parent reference.

**Rule 2 — the return type must be the same or covariant.** The child can return the parent's type or a subtype of it. If the parent returns `Animal`, the child may return `Dog`. This is the **covariant return type**, added in Java 5.

**Rule 3 — access can only widen.** A child may make the method more accessible (`protected` to `public`) but never less (`public` to `private` is a compile error), because a caller holding the parent type expects at least the access the parent promised.

**Rule 4 — checked exceptions can only narrow.** The child may throw the same checked exceptions, narrower ones, or none — but never broader or brand-new checked exceptions. Unchecked exceptions are exempt.

**Rule 5 — some methods can't be overridden at all.** `private` methods aren't inherited; a `static` method with the same name is *method hiding*, not overriding; `final` methods are locked by the parent.

> The single most valuable habit is annotating every override with `@Override`. It isn't required, but it tells the compiler to **verify the override** — so a misspelled name or wrong parameter is caught immediately instead of silently becoming a new method that never runs.

sections.title: The Five Overriding Rules — What Can Change and What Cannot
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OR["Method Overriding Rules"] --> R1["1. Signature — MUST match exactly"]
    OR --> R2["2. Return type — same OR covariant subtype"]
    OR --> R3["3. Access modifier — same OR MORE permissive"]
    OR --> R4["4. Checked exceptions — same OR narrower"]
    OR --> R5["5. Cannot override private / static / final"]

    R1 --> R1E["@Override catches mismatches at compile time"]
    R2 --> R2E["Parent returns Animal → child can return Dog (Java 5+)"]
    R3 --> R3E["protected→public: OK | public→private: compile error"]
    R4 --> R4E["IOException→FileNotFoundException: OK | IOException→Exception: error"]
    R5 --> R5E["static method in child = method hiding, NOT overriding"]
```

sections.title: What Can and Cannot Change in an Overriding Method
sections.content:
| Rule | Parent defines | Child is allowed | Child is NOT allowed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Method name | `speak()` | Must be `speak()` | Any other name |
| Parameters | `(String lang)` | Must be `(String lang)` | Different params |
| Return type | `Animal` | `Animal` or `Dog` (covariant) | Unrelated type |
| Access modifier | `protected` | `protected` or `public` | `private` (narrowing) |
| Checked exceptions | `throws IOException` | `throws IOException`, `throws FileNotFoundException`, or nothing | `throws Exception` (broader) |
| Final / private / static | `final void go()` | — | Cannot override at all |

sections.title: Valid and Invalid Overriding — Annotated Examples
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping `@Override`** — a typo in the name or a wrong parameter silently creates a new method; your override never runs and polymorphism quietly breaks with no compiler warning.
- **Narrowing the access modifier** — going from `public` in the parent to `private` in the child is a compile error; you can only keep or widen access.
- **Throwing a broader checked exception** — if the parent throws `IOException`, the child can throw `FileNotFoundException` or nothing, but never `Exception`.
- **Believing static methods can be overridden** — redeclaring a `static` method in a child is method hiding, resolved by the reference type, not dynamic dispatch.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Signature must match** — same method name and exact parameter list; any difference creates a new method, not an override.
- **Covariant return type** — child can return a more specific type (subtype) than parent; added in Java 5.
- **Access modifier widening only** — child can go `protected → public` but never `public → private`; narrowing breaks the parent's contract.
- **Exception narrowing only** — child can throw fewer or narrower checked exceptions than parent; never broader ones.
- **Cannot override** — `private` (not inherited), `static` (method hiding, not overriding), `final` (locked by parent).
- **@Override annotation** — not required but critical; tells the compiler to verify the override, catching signature typos at compile time rather than silently creating a new method.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
For overriding to count, Java enforces **five rules**, all there to keep a child usable wherever the parent is expected:
- **First, the signature has to match exactly** — same name, same parameters; change a parameter and you've quietly written a new overloaded method instead, while the parent's version still runs.
- **Second, the return type must be the same or a subtype** — covariant returns, so if the parent returns `Animal`, the child can return `Dog`.
- **Third, access can only widen** — `protected` to `public` is fine, but `public` down to `private` won't compile, since a caller holding the parent type expects at least the access the parent promised.
- **Fourth, checked exceptions can only narrow** — the child can throw the same, something narrower, or nothing, but never a broader checked exception; unchecked ones are exempt.
- **Fifth, some methods can't be overridden at all** — `private` isn't inherited, `final` is locked, and a `static` method with the same name is method hiding, not overriding.

The point I always stress is `@Override`. It's optional, but it's the **cheapest safety net in Java**: without it, a typo in the name compiles fine and silently creates a new method, so your override never runs and the bug surfaces only at runtime. So my rule is simple — **annotate every override**.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Animal.speak() overridden in Dog; Animal.reproduce() with covariant Dog return type
speakable_v2.hook: Think of overriding as a contract. The child can widen it, but never breaks it. It honours everything the parent promised.

beats.text: Method overriding means a child class replaces a method it inherited, using the same signature. It's the engine behind runtime polymorphism. Java enforces five strict rules so a child stays safe to use wherever the parent fits.

Why so many rules? They keep a child usable anywhere its parent works. That's the Liskov Substitution Principle. Break a rule and a caller holding the parent type gets a nasty surprise at runtime. The rules simply protect that promise.

items: Rule one. The signature must match exactly. Same name, same parameter list.
Rule two. The return type stays the same, or a covariant subtype. Parent returns `Animal`, child can return `Dog`.
Rule three. Access can only widen. protected to public works, but public to private won't compile.
Rule four. Checked exceptions can only narrow. The child throws the same, fewer, or none.
Rule five. You cannot override private, static, or final methods.

beats.text: Say `Animal` defines a protected reproduce method returning Animal. The child `Dog` overrides it as a public method returning Dog. That widens access for rule three. It also uses a covariant return for rule two. Here's the **non-obvious** habit: always add the override annotation. Skip it and a typo silently creates a brand-new method.

items: Narrowing access, public down to private, breaks the parent's contract. It won't compile.
Skip the override annotation and a typo creates a new method silently. Your polymorphism breaks at runtime with no warning.

speakable_v2.cap: Always add `@Override`. It's the cheapest way to catch overriding mistakes at compile time, instead of debugging them at runtime.
